about: Bioregulatory Systems Year 1 (MEDI40002) is the largest Year 1 module of Imperial's MBBS/BSc: a 20-credit core module running through the autumn and spring terms, according to the 2026-27 programme specification, which also cites Bioregulatory Systems as an example of a module made up of more than one assessment. An unofficial students' union page (last updated in 2022, so possibly out of date) describes it as covering neurology and neuroscience, psychiatry, endocrinology and reproduction, respiratory and cardiovascular medicine, gastroenterology and urology through lectures, tutorials and labs. No official topic list or teaching order is published, so the topics here follow those systems. Phase 1 knowledge is assessed with single best answer, very short answer and/or short answer questions, and every module must be passed; check your module handbook for the exact assessment format.
topics: Neurophysiology: membrane potentials, action potentials and synapses
Organisation of the nervous system: sensory, motor and autonomic pathways
Psychiatry: brain, behaviour and mental disorder
Endocrinology: hormones, the pituitary, thyroid and adrenal glands
Reproduction: the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis and the menstrual cycle
Respiratory physiology: ventilation, gas exchange and control of breathing
Cardiovascular physiology: the heart, cardiac output and blood pressure
Gastrointestinal physiology: digestion, absorption and the liver
Renal and urinary physiology: filtration, tubular function, fluid balance and acid–base

notes.h: Membrane potentials, action potentials and synapses
notes.body:
Excitable cells (neurons and muscle) signal using rapid changes in membrane potential. This topic underpins neurology, cardiology and pharmacology.

Resting membrane potential
- A typical neuron rests at about −70 mV (inside negative).
- The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase keeps K⁺ high inside and Na⁺ high outside. At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ (leak channels), so K⁺ diffuses out until the electrical gradient balances the chemical gradient.
- The equilibrium potential for one ion is given by the Nernst equation. At 37 °C: E = (61.5 / z) × log₁₀([ion]out / [ion]in) mV.
- Worked example: K⁺ 4 mmol/L outside, 140 inside: E_K = 61.5 × log₁₀(4/140) = 61.5 × (−1.544) ≈ −95 mV. Na⁺ 145 outside, 12 inside: E_Na ≈ +67 mV.
- The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation combines ions weighted by their permeabilities. Because K⁺ permeability dominates at rest, the resting potential lies close to E_K but is less negative because of a small Na⁺ leak.
- Clinical link: raised plasma K⁺ (hyperkalaemia) reduces the K⁺ gradient and depolarises cells, which can cause dangerous cardiac arrhythmias.

The action potential
- A stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (roughly −55 mV).
- Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open; Na⁺ rushes in, driving the potential towards E_Na (overshoot to about +30 mV). This is positive feedback.
- Na⁺ channels then inactivate, and slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ leaves and the cell repolarises, briefly overshooting below rest (after-hyperpolarisation).
- All-or-none: once threshold is reached, the size of the action potential is fixed. Stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency.
- Absolute refractory period: Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so no new action potential is possible. Relative refractory period: a stronger stimulus is needed. Refractoriness makes conduction one-way.
- Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.

Conduction
Speed rises with axon diameter and with myelination. Myelin (Schwann cells in the PNS, oligodendrocytes in the CNS) insulates the axon so the action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction). Multiple sclerosis damages CNS myelin; Guillain–Barré syndrome typically affects peripheral nerves.

The chemical synapse
1. The action potential reaches the terminal and opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels.
2. Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle fusion (via SNARE proteins) and transmitter release.
3. Transmitter binds postsynaptic receptors: ionotropic (ligand-gated channels, fast, e.g. nicotinic ACh, AMPA glutamate, GABA-A) or metabotropic (G-protein coupled, slower, e.g. muscarinic ACh).
4. The result is an excitatory (EPSP) or inhibitory (IPSP) postsynaptic potential. These sum in time (temporal) and space (spatial) at the axon hillock to decide whether the neuron fires.
5. Signalling ends by enzymatic breakdown (acetylcholinesterase), reuptake (e.g. serotonin and noradrenaline transporters) or diffusion.
Main transmitters: glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the CNS; GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain and glycine in the spinal cord.

Neuromuscular junction
Motor neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors on skeletal muscle, producing an end-plate potential that triggers a muscle action potential. In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies against ACh receptors cause fatigable weakness. Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking ACh release and causing flaccid paralysis.

Exam tips: show the Nernst calculation step by step (ratio, log, multiply), explain the ionic basis of each phase of the action potential, and number the steps of synaptic transmission.

Clinical neurology depends on knowing where pathways run and where they cross, so you can predict the effect of a lesion.

Overall organisation
- Central nervous system: brain and spinal cord. Peripheral nervous system: cranial and spinal nerves and ganglia.
- Somatic system (skeletal muscle, conscious sensation) versus autonomic system (smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands).

Cortex and deeper structures
- Frontal lobe: primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus; personality and planning; Broca's area (expressive language, usually in the left hemisphere).
- Parietal lobe: primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus. The body is mapped as a distorted homunculus, with large areas for hands and face.
- Temporal lobe: hearing, memory (hippocampus), Wernicke's area (understanding language).
- Occipital lobe: vision.
- Basal ganglia: selecting and initiating movement. Parkinson's disease follows loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, giving bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor.
- Cerebellum: coordination; lesions cause ataxia and intention tremor on the same side as the lesion.
- Brainstem: cranial nerve nuclei and centres controlling breathing and circulation.

Ascending (sensory) pathways
- Dorsal column–medial lemniscus: fine touch, vibration and joint position sense. Travels up the same side of the spinal cord and crosses in the medulla.
- Spinothalamic tract: pain and temperature. Crosses within one or two segments of entry, then ascends on the opposite side.
- Consequence: a hemisection of the cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome) gives loss of vibration/proprioception and weakness on the same side below the lesion, and loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side.

Descending (motor) pathway
The corticospinal tract runs from motor cortex through the internal capsule and brainstem; most fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla and descend in the lateral corticospinal tract to synapse on lower motor neurons in the anterior horn.
- Upper motor neuron lesion: weakness, increased tone (spasticity), brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar response, little wasting.
- Lower motor neuron lesion: weakness, wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone and reduced or absent reflexes.

The stretch reflex
Tapping a tendon stretches muscle spindles; Ia afferents synapse directly (monosynaptic) on α motor neurons, which contract the same muscle. The knee jerk tests roughly L3–L4.

Autonomic nervous system
- Sympathetic: outflow from the thoracolumbar cord (T1–L2). Short preganglionic fibres synapse in ganglia near the cord using ACh on nicotinic receptors; most postganglionic fibres release noradrenaline onto adrenergic receptors. Exceptions: sweat glands use ACh, and the adrenal medulla is innervated directly by preganglionic fibres and releases adrenaline into the blood.
- Parasympathetic: craniosacral outflow (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral S2–S4). Long preganglionic fibres synapse in ganglia near or in the target organ; postganglionic fibres release ACh onto muscarinic receptors. The vagus nerve supplies the heart, lungs and most of the gut.
Typical effects:
- Heart: sympathetic raises rate and contractility (β₁); parasympathetic slows rate.
- Pupil: sympathetic dilates; parasympathetic constricts.
- Airways: sympathetic dilates (β₂); parasympathetic constricts.
- Gut: parasympathetic increases motility and secretion; sympathetic reduces them.
- Bladder: parasympathetic contracts the detrusor (voiding); sympathetic relaxes it and contracts the internal sphincter (storage).

Supporting structures
Cerebrospinal fluid is made mainly by the choroid plexus and cushions and nourishes the brain. The blood–brain barrier (tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells, supported by astrocytes) limits entry of many drugs and toxins.

Exam tips: when asked to localise a lesion, list which pathways are affected on which side, and use UMN versus LMN signs. Know the transmitter and receptor at each autonomic synapse.

notes.h: Psychiatry: brain, behaviour and mental disorder
notes.body:
Year 1 psychiatry introduces how mental disorders are described and classified, how to examine mental state, and the biological, psychological and social factors behind them. Much of the biology is still debated, and exams reward knowing which ideas are well supported and which are contested.

Classification and models
- Two systems are used: the WHO's International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11 came into effect in January 2022) and the American Psychiatric Association's DSM (DSM-5-TR, 2022).
- The biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977) argues that illness should be understood through biological, psychological and social factors together, not biology alone.
- The stress–vulnerability (diathesis–stress) model: an underlying vulnerability (genetic, developmental) combines with stressors to trigger illness.

The mental state examination (MSE)
The psychiatric equivalent of a physical examination, recorded under headings:
- Appearance and behaviour
- Speech (rate, volume, quantity)
- Mood (subjective) and affect (what the clinician observes)
- Thought form (e.g. flight of ideas, loosening of associations) and thought content (e.g. delusions, preoccupations, thoughts of self-harm)
- Perception (hallucinations, illusions)
- Cognition (orientation, attention, memory)
- Insight (does the person recognise they are unwell?)
Risk to self and others is assessed alongside.

Key definitions
- Delusion: a fixed, false belief held with conviction despite evidence to the contrary and not explained by the person's cultural or religious background.
- Hallucination: a perception without an external stimulus (e.g. hearing voices when no one is speaking).
- Illusion: a misinterpretation of a real stimulus.
- Psychosis: loss of contact with reality, typically with delusions and/or hallucinations.

Depression
Core features are persistent low mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) lasting at least two weeks, with other symptoms such as fatigue, sleep and appetite change, poor concentration, guilt or worthlessness and thoughts of death.
Biology (contested):
- The monoamine hypothesis, developed in the 1960s, proposed that depression reflects low serotonin and/or noradrenaline, partly because drugs raising monoamines relieve symptoms.
- Problems with the simple version: antidepressants raise synaptic monoamines within hours but clinical benefit usually takes weeks, and a 2022 umbrella review (Moncrieff and colleagues) found no consistent evidence of reduced serotonin in depression. That review has itself been criticised, and antidepressants still show benefit in trials, so the debate continues.
- Other proposed contributors include HPA-axis overactivity (raised cortisol in some patients), reduced neuroplasticity and inflammation. None is accepted as the single cause.

Schizophrenia and dopamine
- Positive symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder. Negative symptoms: reduced motivation, emotional blunting, social withdrawal. Cognitive impairment is also common.
- Dopamine hypothesis: excess dopamine signalling in mesolimbic/striatal pathways is linked to positive symptoms. Support: antipsychotics block D₂ receptors and stimulants such as amphetamine can cause psychosis. Later versions (e.g. Howes and Kapur, 2009) emphasise increased presynaptic dopamine synthesis in the striatum as a final common pathway.
- Limits: the hypothesis explains negative and cognitive symptoms poorly, and glutamate (NMDA-receptor hypofunction) theories are also proposed. Treat dopamine as part of the story, not the whole.

Anxiety and the stress response
Threat activates the amygdala, the sympathetic nervous system (fight or flight: tachycardia, sweating, tremor) and the HPA axis (CRH → ACTH → cortisol, with negative feedback). Persistent or excessive activation of these threat systems is thought to contribute to anxiety disorders such as generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder, though no single mechanism explains them.

Exam tips: use correct terms in an MSE (mood versus affect; delusion versus overvalued idea), and when discussing biological theories, give the supporting evidence and the main criticisms rather than stating a single cause.

notes.h: Hormones, the pituitary, thyroid and adrenal glands
notes.body:
Endocrine systems control slower, longer-lasting processes than nerves. Exams test hormone classes, axes, feedback and how to interpret simple hormone results.

Hormone classes
- Peptide/protein hormones (e.g. insulin, ADH, ACTH): water-soluble, stored in vesicles, act on cell-surface receptors (G-protein coupled with second messengers such as cAMP or IP₃, or receptor tyrosine kinases for insulin).
- Steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, oestradiol, testosterone): made from cholesterol on demand, carried bound to proteins, cross membranes and act on intracellular receptors that change gene transcription, so their effects are slower.
- Amines: catecholamines behave like peptides (surface receptors); thyroid hormones behave like steroids (nuclear receptors).

Feedback
Negative feedback is the rule: rising hormone levels suppress the hypothalamus and pituitary. Positive feedback is rare: the mid-cycle LH surge and oxytocin during labour.

The hypothalamus and pituitary
- Anterior pituitary: controlled by hypothalamic hormones carried in the hypophyseal portal circulation. TRH → TSH; CRH → ACTH; GnRH → LH and FSH; GHRH → GH (somatostatin inhibits GH). Prolactin is mainly under inhibitory control by dopamine, so damage to the pituitary stalk raises prolactin.
- Posterior pituitary: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are made in hypothalamic neurons (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei) and released from their axon terminals.

Thyroid
- TRH → TSH → thyroid secretes mainly T4 with some T3; much T4 is converted to the more active T3 in tissues. Iodine is essential.
- Actions: raise basal metabolic rate and heat production, increase heart rate and sensitivity to catecholamines, and are vital for growth and brain development.
- Primary hypothyroidism (commonly autoimmune Hashimoto's thyroiditis in the UK; iodine deficiency worldwide): low T4 with high TSH because feedback is lost. Features: tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia.
- Graves' disease: antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor, giving high T4/T3 and suppressed TSH; features include weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, and eye signs specific to Graves'.

Adrenal glands
Cortex (outer to inner):
- Zona glomerulosa: aldosterone, controlled mainly by the renin–angiotensin system and plasma K⁺.
- Zona fasciculata: cortisol, controlled by ACTH.
- Zona reticularis: adrenal androgens.
Medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline, released on sympathetic stimulation.
Cortisol: secreted with a circadian rhythm (highest in the early morning); raises blood glucose (gluconeogenesis), breaks down protein, suppresses inflammation and immunity, and supports blood pressure. Excess (Cushing's syndrome) causes central weight gain, proximal muscle weakness, thin skin, hypertension and hyperglycaemia. Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) causes fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, low sodium and high potassium (from aldosterone loss) and skin pigmentation (high ACTH acting on melanocortin receptors).

Calcium regulation
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises plasma calcium: it increases bone resorption, increases calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron and stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase to make calcitriol, which increases intestinal calcium absorption. Low calcium stimulates PTH release.

Reading results: primary or secondary?
- Primary gland failure: low target hormone, high pituitary hormone (e.g. low T4, high TSH).
- Secondary (pituitary) failure: low target hormone with low or inappropriately normal pituitary hormone.
- Primary overactivity: high target hormone, suppressed pituitary hormone.

Exam tips: draw the axis with arrows and feedback loops before answering, and always interpret a hormone level alongside its controlling hormone.

notes.h: The hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis and the menstrual cycle
notes.body:
Reproductive endocrinology is a favourite source of data-interpretation and sequence questions. Learn the axis, the cycle in order and where positive feedback fits.

The axis
- The hypothalamus releases GnRH in pulses. Pulsatile GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH.
- Continuous (non-pulsatile) GnRH exposure does the opposite: after an initial surge it suppresses LH and FSH. This is used therapeutically, for example to lower testosterone in prostate cancer.

Male reproductive physiology
- LH acts on Leydig cells in the testis to produce testosterone.
- FSH, together with high local testosterone, acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules.
- Sertoli cells produce inhibin B, which feeds back to reduce FSH; testosterone feeds back to reduce GnRH and LH.
- Spermatogenesis takes roughly two to two and a half months from stem cell to mature sperm, so a factor affecting sperm production shows up in semen analysis weeks later.

The ovarian cycle (average 28 days; length varies mainly because the follicular phase varies)
Follicular phase (from day 1 of menstruation to ovulation):
- FSH recruits a group of follicles; one becomes dominant.
- Two-cell model: theca cells, under LH, make androgens; granulosa cells, under FSH, convert them to oestradiol using aromatase.
- Moderate oestradiol and inhibin exert negative feedback on FSH, so the non-dominant follicles regress.
Ovulation:
- When oestradiol is high and sustained, its feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary switches from negative to positive, producing the LH surge.
- The LH surge triggers final maturation and ovulation, which follows roughly a day and a half after the surge begins (around day 14 of a 28-day cycle).
Luteal phase (about 14 days, fairly constant):
- The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone and oestradiol, which suppress GnRH, LH and FSH.
- Without pregnancy, the corpus luteum regresses after about two weeks; progesterone and oestradiol fall, FSH starts to rise, and the next cycle begins.
- If an embryo implants, the trophoblast secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum alive and producing progesterone. Detection of hCG is the basis of pregnancy tests.

The endometrial (uterine) cycle
- Menstrual phase: shedding of the functional layer when progesterone falls.
- Proliferative phase: oestradiol rebuilds the endometrium (matches the follicular phase).
- Secretory phase: progesterone makes the endometrium glandular and receptive for implantation (matches the luteal phase).
Progesterone also raises basal body temperature slightly and thickens cervical mucus.

Fertilisation and early pregnancy
Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The embryo implants in the endometrium about a week after fertilisation.

Menopause
Ovarian follicles are depleted, so oestradiol and inhibin fall and, with negative feedback lost, FSH and LH rise. In the UK it usually happens between 45 and 55, with an average age of about 51. Lower oestrogen contributes to vasomotor symptoms and loss of bone density.

Hormonal contraception (mechanism only)
Combined hormonal contraception supplies oestrogen and progestogen that suppress GnRH, FSH and LH by negative feedback, so no follicle reaches ovulation; progestogens also thicken cervical mucus.

Exam tips: draw hormone levels against cycle day, mark the LH surge just before ovulation and the progesterone peak in the mid-luteal phase, and explain the switch from negative to positive feedback.

notes.h: Ventilation, gas exchange and control of breathing
notes.body:
Respiratory physiology combines mechanics, gas laws and control systems. Many questions include calculations, so practise them.

Mechanics of breathing
- Inspiration is active: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostals raise the ribs. Thoracic volume increases, so intrapleural and alveolar pressures fall (Boyle's law) and air flows in.
- Quiet expiration is passive, driven by elastic recoil of the lungs; forced expiration uses abdominal and internal intercostal muscles.
- Intrapleural pressure is normally negative relative to the atmosphere, keeping the lungs expanded. If air enters the pleural space (pneumothorax), the lung recoils and collapses.

Compliance and surfactant
- Compliance = change in volume ÷ change in pressure. Fibrosis reduces it (stiff lungs); emphysema increases it but loses elastic recoil, so airways collapse on expiration.
- Surface tension in alveoli tends to collapse them; by the Laplace relation (P = 2T/r) smaller alveoli would collapse into larger ones. Surfactant from type II pneumocytes lowers surface tension, especially in small alveoli. Premature babies lacking surfactant develop neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

Airway resistance and spirometry
- Resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴ (Poiseuille). Halving airway radius increases resistance 16-fold, so modest narrowing in asthma has a large effect.
- Obstructive pattern (asthma, COPD): FEV₁ reduced more than FVC, so FEV₁/FVC is below 0.7.
- Restrictive pattern (e.g. pulmonary fibrosis): FVC reduced with a normal or high FEV₁/FVC.

Ventilation
- Minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate: 0.5 L × 12/min = 6 L/min.
- Anatomical dead space (about 150 mL) does not take part in gas exchange. Alveolar ventilation = (0.5 − 0.15) × 12 = 4.2 L/min.
- Rapid shallow breathing wastes a bigger fraction of each breath on dead space.

Gas exchange
- Diffusion across the alveolar membrane follows Fick's law; thickening (fibrosis) or loss of surface area (emphysema) impairs it.
- Alveolar gas equation: PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (Patm − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/R. Breathing air at sea level: 0.21 × (101.3 − 6.3) − 5.3/0.8 ≈ 19.95 − 6.63 ≈ 13.3 kPa.
- Ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) matching: a shunt is perfusion without ventilation (e.g. pneumonia filling alveoli) and responds poorly to extra oxygen; dead space is ventilation without perfusion (e.g. pulmonary embolism). Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated areas.

Gas transport
- O₂ content ≈ (1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + dissolved O₂. With Hb 15 g/dL and SaO₂ 98%: 1.34 × 15 × 0.98 ≈ 19.7 mL/dL, plus about 0.3 mL/dL dissolved (0.003 mL/dL per mmHg × 100 mmHg) ≈ 20 mL O₂ per 100 mL blood. Almost all O₂ travels bound to haemoglobin.
- CO₂ travels mostly as bicarbonate (formed in red cells by carbonic anhydrase, with the chloride shift), with smaller amounts as carbamino compounds and dissolved CO₂. Deoxygenated blood carries more CO₂ (Haldane effect).

Control of breathing
- Rhythm is generated in the medulla (with pontine input).
- Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H⁺ in the CSF, which reflects arterial PCO₂; this is the main minute-to-minute drive.
- Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies, via the glossopharyngeal nerve; aortic bodies, via the vagus) respond mainly to low PaO₂, becoming important below about 8 kPa, and also to raised PCO₂ and H⁺.

Respiratory failure (blood gases)
Typical reference values: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ about 4.7–6.0 kPa, PaO₂ above about 10.6 kPa on air. Type 1 respiratory failure: PaO₂ below 8 kPa with normal or low PaCO₂ (V/Q mismatch). Type 2: PaO₂ below 8 kPa with raised PaCO₂ (ventilatory failure).

Exam tips: write out equations before substituting, keep units consistent (kPa throughout), and link spirometry patterns to the underlying mechanics.

notes.h: The heart, cardiac output and blood pressure
notes.body:
Cardiovascular physiology links electrical events, mechanical events and the control of pressure and flow.

Electrical activity
- The sinoatrial (SA) node sets the rate. Its cells have no stable resting potential: a slow inward "funny" current (through HCN channels) depolarises them to threshold, and the upstroke is carried by Ca²⁺.
- The impulse spreads across the atria to the atrioventricular (AV) node, where conduction is delayed (about 0.1 s) so the ventricles fill, then down the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres.
- Ventricular myocyte action potential: phase 0 rapid Na⁺ influx; phase 1 brief repolarisation; phase 2 plateau, maintained by Ca²⁺ entry through L-type channels; phase 3 repolarisation by K⁺ efflux; phase 4 resting. Ca²⁺ entering in phase 2 triggers further Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release), causing contraction. The long plateau and refractory period prevent tetany.
- ECG: P wave = atrial depolarisation; PR interval = conduction through the AV node (normally 0.12–0.20 s); QRS = ventricular depolarisation (normally under 0.12 s); T wave = ventricular repolarisation.

The cardiac cycle
1. Atrial systole tops up ventricular filling.
2. Isovolumetric contraction: ventricles contract with all valves closed; closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves gives the first heart sound.
3. Ejection: aortic and pulmonary valves open once ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure.
4. Isovolumetric relaxation: closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves gives the second heart sound.
5. Ventricular filling, mostly passive.

Cardiac output
- Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Example: 70 beats/min × 70 mL = 4.9 L/min.
- Ejection fraction = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume, e.g. 70/120 ≈ 58%.
- Stroke volume depends on:
  - Preload: greater end-diastolic stretch increases force of contraction (Frank–Starling law), matching output to venous return.
  - Afterload: the pressure the ventricle must eject against; higher afterload lowers stroke volume.
  - Contractility: increased by sympathetic stimulation (β₁ receptors raise Ca²⁺ entry).
- Fick principle: cardiac output = O₂ consumption ÷ arteriovenous O₂ difference. With 250 mL O₂/min and arterial and mixed venous contents of 200 and 150 mL/L: 250/50 = 5 L/min.

Pressure, flow and resistance
- Mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≈ cardiac output × total peripheral resistance (strictly, the pressure drop from MAP to right atrial pressure, which is close to zero).
- At normal heart rates MAP ≈ diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure: for 120/80 mmHg, 80 + 40/3 ≈ 93 mmHg.
- Resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴, so arterioles, whose radius is adjusted by smooth muscle, control resistance and distribution of flow.

Short-term control: the baroreflex
Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus nerve) signal to the medulla. A rise in pressure increases vagal activity and reduces sympathetic activity, slowing the heart and dilating vessels. On standing, blood pools in the legs, pressure falls briefly, and the reflex raises heart rate and vasoconstriction within seconds. Failure of this response causes postural hypotension.

Long-term control
The kidneys control blood volume. The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ADH conserve salt and water when pressure or volume falls; natriuretic peptides from stretched atria and ventricles promote salt excretion.

Capillary exchange and oedema
Starling forces govern fluid movement: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out; plasma oncotic pressure (mainly albumin) holds it in. Oedema results from raised capillary hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous obstruction), low plasma albumin (liver disease, nephrotic syndrome), increased permeability (inflammation) or blocked lymphatics.

Exam tips: show formulae before numbers, link each heart sound to valve closure, and use the baroreflex as a worked example of negative feedback.

The gut breaks food into absorbable units, absorbs them and controls this with nerves and hormones. The liver processes what is absorbed.

Structure and control
- Wall layers: mucosa, submucosa (containing the submucosal or Meissner's plexus), muscularis externa (with the myenteric or Auerbach's plexus between its layers) and serosa.
- The enteric nervous system can run local reflexes on its own; the vagus nerve increases secretion and motility, sympathetic activity reduces them.
- Motility patterns: peristalsis propels contents; segmentation mixes them; the migrating motor complex sweeps the small intestine between meals.

Mouth and oesophagus
Salivary amylase starts starch digestion. Swallowing moves the bolus into the oesophagus; the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to let it into the stomach and normally prevents reflux.

Stomach
- Parietal cells secrete H⁺ via the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (the proton pump) and intrinsic factor.
- Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, converted to pepsin at low pH.
- G cells in the antrum release gastrin; D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits acid.
- Acid secretion is stimulated by ACh (vagus), gastrin and histamine (from enterochromaffin-like cells, acting on H₂ receptors). Phases: cephalic (sight and thought of food), gastric (distension, peptides) and intestinal.
- The mucosa is protected by mucus and bicarbonate and by prostaglandins. Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAIDs (which reduce prostaglandin synthesis) are the main causes of peptic ulcers.

Pancreas and bile
- Acid entering the duodenum releases secretin (from S cells), which stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice to neutralise it.
- Fat and protein release cholecystokinin (CCK, from I cells), which stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.
- Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive precursors: enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal brush border activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which activates the others.
- Bile salts emulsify fat and form micelles; most are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver (enterohepatic circulation).

Absorption
- Carbohydrate: absorbed as monosaccharides. Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes with Na⁺ via SGLT1; fructose by facilitated diffusion via GLUT5; all leave via GLUT2.
- Protein: absorbed as amino acids and as di- and tripeptides (via PepT1).
- Fat: monoglycerides and fatty acids enter enterocytes from micelles, are re-made into triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons, which enter lacteals (lymph) rather than portal blood.
- Sites to remember: iron mainly in the duodenum; vitamin B12 (with intrinsic factor) and bile salts in the terminal ileum. Most water is absorbed in the small intestine; the colon absorbs further water and Na⁺.

The liver
Functions: makes albumin and most clotting factors; stores glycogen and makes glucose; makes bile; metabolises drugs and hormones; converts ammonia to urea.
Bilirubin handling:
- Haem from old red cells → unconjugated bilirubin (fat-soluble, carried on albumin).
- The liver conjugates it with glucuronic acid (UDP-glucuronyl transferase), making it water-soluble, and excretes it in bile.
- Gut bacteria turn it into urobilinogen, some of which is reabsorbed; stercobilin colours stools.
Jaundice types:
- Pre-hepatic (e.g. haemolysis): excess unconjugated bilirubin; urine colour normal.
- Hepatic (e.g. hepatitis): mixed picture.
- Post-hepatic or obstructive (e.g. gallstone in the common bile duct, pancreatic head cancer): conjugated bilirubin backs up into blood and spills into urine (dark urine), and less reaches the gut (pale stools).

Clinical link: coeliac disease
An immune reaction to gluten damages the proximal small intestine (villous atrophy), causing malabsorption; iron and folate deficiency are common presentations.

notes.h: Filtration, tubular function, fluid balance and acid–base
notes.body:
The kidneys regulate fluid volume, electrolytes, acid–base balance and blood pressure, and excrete waste. The urinary tract stores and voids urine.

Key numbers (typical adult)
- Renal blood flow is about 20–25% of cardiac output; renal plasma flow about 600 mL/min.
- Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) about 120 mL/min (roughly 170–180 L/day), so filtration fraction ≈ 120/600 = 0.2.

Glomerular filtration
- Driven by Starling forces: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out; Bowman's space pressure and plasma oncotic pressure oppose it.
- Autoregulation keeps GFR fairly stable over a wide range of pressures by the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback (the macula densa senses NaCl delivery and adjusts afferent arteriolar tone).
- Afferent arteriolar constriction lowers GFR; efferent constriction raises glomerular pressure and GFR. Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, which helps maintain GFR when perfusion is low; this is why blocking the renin–angiotensin system can reduce GFR in renal artery stenosis.

Clearance
Clearance = (U × V) / P, where U is urine concentration, V urine flow rate and P plasma concentration.
- Worked example: U = 12 mg/mL, V = 1 mL/min, P = 0.1 mg/mL → clearance = 12/0.1 = 120 mL/min.
- Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR. Creatinine approximates GFR but slightly overestimates it because some is secreted. In practice an estimated GFR is calculated from serum creatinine.

The tubule
- Proximal convoluted tubule: reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered Na⁺ and water, nearly all filtered glucose (mainly via SGLT2) and amino acids, and most filtered bicarbonate. Glucose appears in urine when the filtered load (GFR × plasma glucose; e.g. 0.12 L/min × 5 mmol/L = 0.6 mmol/min) exceeds transport capacity, which happens when plasma glucose rises well above normal (roughly 10 mmol/L).
- Loop of Henle: the descending limb is permeable to water; the thick ascending limb pumps out Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ (NKCC2) but is impermeable to water. This countercurrent multiplier builds a concentrated medulla. Loop diuretics block NKCC2.
- Distal convoluted tubule: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ reabsorbed via NCC (blocked by thiazides); PTH increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption here.
- Collecting duct: principal cells reabsorb Na⁺ through ENaC and secrete K⁺, both increased by aldosterone. ADH acts on V₂ receptors to insert aquaporin-2 channels, so water is drawn into the concentrated medulla and urine is concentrated. Intercalated cells secrete H⁺ or bicarbonate.

Hormonal control
- Renin, released from juxtaglomerular cells when renal perfusion falls, when less NaCl reaches the macula densa or with sympathetic (β₁) stimulation, converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (largely in the lung) makes angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles, stimulates aldosterone, ADH and thirst, and increases proximal Na⁺ reabsorption.
- ADH is released mainly in response to raised plasma osmolality (hypothalamic osmoreceptors) and also to a large fall in blood volume.
- Natriuretic peptides promote Na⁺ excretion.

Acid–base
- Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻] / (0.23 × PaCO₂ in kPa)). With HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L and PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa: 24 / 1.219 ≈ 19.7; log₁₀ ≈ 1.29; pH ≈ 7.39.
- The kidney reclaims filtered bicarbonate and makes new bicarbonate by excreting H⁺ as titratable acid (mainly phosphate) and as ammonium.
- Compensation: the lungs compensate for metabolic disorders within minutes to hours (deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing in diabetic ketoacidosis); the kidneys compensate for respiratory disorders over days.
- Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). A raised gap in metabolic acidosis suggests unmeasured anions such as lactate or ketones.

Micturition
The bladder fills under sympathetic influence (detrusor relaxed, internal sphincter contracted) with voluntary control of the external sphincter via the pudendal nerve. Voiding is coordinated by the pontine micturition centre: parasympathetic fibres (S2–S4) contract the detrusor while the sphincters relax.

Exam tips: state the clearance formula with units, know where each diuretic class acts, and analyse blood gases in order: pH, then PaCO₂, then bicarbonate, then compensation.

questions.q: Extracellular K⁺ is 4 mmol/L and intracellular K⁺ is 140 mmol/L. Using E = 61.5 log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV, what is E_K?
questions.why: log₁₀(4/140) = −1.544, and 61.5 × −1.544 ≈ −95 mV. +95 mV comes from inverting the ratio (inside over outside). +1.8 mV comes from multiplying 61.5 by the ratio itself (4/140 ≈ 0.029) instead of by its logarithm. −219 mV comes from using the natural log (ln(4/140) ≈ −3.56) with the 61.5 constant, which already includes the conversion to log₁₀.

questions.q: What directly triggers neurotransmitter release from a presynaptic terminal?
options: Ca²⁺ entry through voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Binding of transmitter to presynaptic autoreceptors
questions.why: When the action potential depolarises the terminal, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open, and the rise in intracellular Ca²⁺ drives SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion. Na⁺ entry through ligand-gated channels happens on the postsynaptic side, producing the EPSP, not release. K⁺ efflux repolarises the membrane and would reduce release. Autoreceptors usually provide feedback inhibition of release; they do not trigger it.

questions.q: Describe the ionic events of a neuronal action potential and explain why it is all-or-none.
markScheme: Depolarisation to threshold (about −55 mV) opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Na⁺ influx causes further depolarisation (positive feedback), overshooting towards E_Na
Na⁺ channels inactivate; voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ efflux repolarises
After-hyperpolarisation as K⁺ channels close slowly; Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains gradients
All-or-none: once threshold is reached the regenerative Na⁺ influx produces a full spike of fixed size; below threshold none occurs
questions.modelAnswer: A stimulus depolarises the membrane from about −70 mV. If it reaches threshold, about −55 mV, enough voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open that Na⁺ influx depolarises the membrane further, opening still more channels. This positive feedback drives the potential rapidly towards the Na⁺ equilibrium potential, overshooting to about +30 mV. The Na⁺ channels then inactivate, and slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ leaves and the membrane repolarises, briefly undershooting the resting potential because the K⁺ channels close slowly. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains the gradients over time. The spike is all-or-none because once threshold is crossed the regenerative Na⁺ influx always produces a full-sized action potential, whereas below threshold K⁺ efflux wins and no spike occurs; stimulus strength is coded by frequency rather than size.

questions.q: A stab wound hemisects the left side of the spinal cord at T10. Which finding is expected below the lesion?
options: Loss of pain and temperature on the left
Loss of vibration sense on the right
Loss of pain and temperature on the right
questions.why: Spinothalamic fibres cross within one or two segments of entry, so the left-sided tract carries pain and temperature from the right: loss is on the right. Dorsal columns ascend on the same side and cross in the medulla, so vibration is lost on the left, not the right. The corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla, so weakness is on the same (left) side. Pain and temperature loss on the left would only occur if the spinothalamic tract did not cross in the cord.

questions.q: Which feature indicates a lower motor neuron lesion rather than an upper motor neuron lesion?
questions.why: Damage to the lower motor neuron denervates muscle, causing wasting and spontaneous twitching (fasciculations), with reduced tone and reflexes. An upgoing plantar response, spasticity and brisk reflexes all reflect loss of descending inhibition, so they are upper motor neuron signs.

questions.q: Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions in terms of outflow, ganglion position and neurotransmitters, and give one opposing effect on the heart.
markScheme: Sympathetic: thoracolumbar (T1–L2); ganglia near cord; short pre-, long postganglionic
Parasympathetic: craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X; S2–S4); ganglia near/in target; long pre-, short postganglionic
Both use ACh at nicotinic ganglionic receptors; sympathetic postganglionic mostly noradrenaline (exceptions: sweat glands, adrenal medulla); parasympathetic postganglionic ACh at muscarinic receptors
Heart: sympathetic (β₁) raises rate and contractility; vagus slows rate
questions.modelAnswer: The sympathetic system leaves the cord from T1 to L2; its preganglionic fibres are short and synapse in ganglia close to the cord (the sympathetic chain or prevertebral ganglia), and the postganglionic fibres are long. The parasympathetic system leaves via cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and sacral segments S2–S4; its preganglionic fibres are long and synapse in ganglia near or within the target organ. In both, preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors. Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline onto adrenergic receptors (sweat glands use ACh, and the adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline), whereas parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release ACh onto muscarinic receptors. In the heart, sympathetic stimulation via β₁ receptors raises heart rate and contractility, while vagal (parasympathetic) activity slows the rate.

questions.q: A patient says that a television presenter is sending him personal messages, and he cannot be persuaded otherwise despite clear evidence. Which term best describes this?
questions.why: A fixed false belief held despite contrary evidence and not explained by culture is a delusion (here a delusion of reference). A hallucination is a perception without a stimulus, but he is describing a belief about real broadcasts, not a false perception. An illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus, such as mistaking a coat for a person. An obsession is an intrusive thought the person recognises as coming from their own mind and usually resists, unlike this firmly held belief.

questions.q: Which observation is most often cited as a problem for the simple monoamine hypothesis of depression?
options: Antidepressants have no effect on synaptic serotonin
Antidepressants raise synaptic monoamines within hours but mood usually improves only after weeks
Depression never responds to drug treatment
Monoamines are not found in the human brain
questions.why: SSRIs block serotonin reuptake quickly, so if low serotonin alone caused depression, improvement should be fast; the delay of weeks suggests downstream changes (such as neuroplasticity) matter, which is why the simple hypothesis is contested. The claim that antidepressants do not affect synaptic serotonin is false: blocking reuptake raises it. The claim that depression never responds to drugs is false; trials show benefit, which is why the debate continues. Serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine are all present in the brain, so that option misstates basic neurochemistry.

questions.q: Outline the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia, giving evidence for it and its main limitations.
markScheme: States that excess dopamine signalling in mesolimbic/striatal pathways underlies positive symptoms
Evidence: antipsychotic efficacy linked to D₂ blockade
Evidence: dopamine-releasing stimulants (amphetamine) can cause psychosis; imaging shows raised presynaptic striatal dopamine synthesis (later versions)
Limitation: explains negative and cognitive symptoms poorly; not all patients respond to D₂ blockade
Alternative/complementary: glutamate NMDA hypofunction; biopsychosocial factors
questions.modelAnswer: The dopamine hypothesis proposes that overactive dopamine signalling in mesolimbic and striatal pathways produces the positive symptoms of schizophrenia, such as delusions and hallucinations. Supporting evidence includes the fact that antipsychotic drugs share the property of blocking D₂ receptors, and that drugs which increase dopamine release, such as amphetamine, can cause psychotic symptoms in healthy people and worsen them in patients. Later versions, such as that of Howes and Kapur (2009), draw on imaging showing increased presynaptic dopamine synthesis in the striatum. The hypothesis has limitations: it explains negative and cognitive symptoms poorly, some patients do not respond to D₂ blockade, and it does not say why dopamine becomes dysregulated. Glutamate (NMDA-receptor hypofunction) theories and social and developmental factors are proposed as complementary explanations, so dopamine is best seen as one part of the picture.

questions.q: Blood tests show a low free T4 with a raised TSH. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Excess TRH from a hypothalamic tumour
questions.why: When the thyroid itself fails, low T4 removes negative feedback, so the pituitary raises TSH: primary hypothyroidism. Pituitary failure would give low T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH, not a high one. Graves' disease gives high T4 with suppressed TSH, the opposite pattern. Excess TRH would drive TSH up, but the thyroid would then respond with high T4, not low.

questions.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex produces aldosterone?
questions.why: The outermost zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone, controlled mainly by angiotensin II and plasma K⁺. The zona fasciculata makes cortisol under ACTH, so choosing it confuses the glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid layers. The zona reticularis makes adrenal androgens. The medulla is not cortex at all and releases adrenaline and noradrenaline.

questions.q: A patient has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease). Explain the expected changes in cortisol, ACTH, aldosterone, plasma sodium and potassium, and skin colour.
markScheme: Adrenal cortex destroyed (commonly autoimmune in the UK): low cortisol
Loss of cortisol negative feedback: high ACTH
Low aldosterone (zona glomerulosa also affected)
Low aldosterone: reduced Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion in collecting duct → hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, volume depletion/hypotension
High ACTH stimulates melanocortin receptors → hyperpigmentation
questions.modelAnswer: In primary adrenal insufficiency the adrenal cortex itself is damaged, so cortisol is low. Without cortisol's negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, CRH and ACTH rise. The zona glomerulosa is also affected, so aldosterone is low. Without aldosterone, principal cells in the collecting duct reabsorb less sodium and secrete less potassium, so plasma sodium falls, potassium rises, and salt and water loss causes volume depletion and low blood pressure. The high ACTH also acts on melanocortin receptors in the skin, causing increased pigmentation, for example in skin creases and the mouth.

questions.q: What is the immediate trigger for ovulation in a normal menstrual cycle?
questions.why: Sustained high oestradiol from the dominant follicle switches to positive feedback, producing the mid-cycle LH surge, which triggers ovulation. A fall in progesterone, when the corpus luteum regresses, triggers menstruation, not ovulation. hCG rises only after implantation and maintains the corpus luteum. Oestradiol rises to a peak that sets off the LH surge; it then falls during the surge, before ovulation, as the follicle luteinises, so its fall is a consequence of the surge, not the trigger for ovulation.

questions.q: In the testis, which cells produce testosterone in response to LH?
questions.why: Leydig cells lie between the seminiferous tubules and make testosterone under LH. Sertoli cells respond to FSH and support spermatogenesis, so choosing them swaps the targets of LH and FSH. Granulosa and theca cells are ovarian, not testicular; theca cells are the ovarian counterpart that make androgens under LH, which is why they can be confused with Leydig cells.

questions.q: Describe the hormonal changes across the luteal phase and explain what happens if fertilisation does and does not occur.
markScheme: After ovulation the follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone (and oestradiol)
Progesterone peaks mid-luteal; makes endometrium secretory; negative feedback suppresses LH/FSH
Luteal phase about 14 days, fairly constant
No pregnancy: corpus luteum regresses; progesterone and oestradiol fall; menstruation; FSH rises for next cycle
Pregnancy: trophoblast hCG maintains the corpus luteum and its progesterone
questions.modelAnswer: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone and oestradiol. Progesterone peaks in the middle of the luteal phase; it converts the endometrium to a secretory, receptive state and, with oestradiol, suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH by negative feedback. The luteal phase lasts about 14 days and is fairly constant between cycles. If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum regresses, progesterone and oestradiol fall, the functional endometrium is shed (menstruation), and release from negative feedback allows FSH to rise and recruit follicles for the next cycle. If an embryo implants, the trophoblast secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum alive so progesterone continues to support the endometrium.

questions.q: A person breathes with a tidal volume of 0.5 L at 12 breaths/min, with an anatomical dead space of 0.15 L. What is the alveolar ventilation?
questions.why: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate = (0.5 − 0.15) × 12 = 4.2 L/min. 6.0 L/min is total minute ventilation, ignoring dead space. 1.8 L/min is dead-space ventilation (0.15 × 12), the part that does not reach alveoli. 7.8 L/min comes from adding dead space instead of subtracting it ((0.5 + 0.15) × 12).

questions.q: Spirometry shows FEV₁ 1.5 L and FVC 3.5 L. Which pattern is this?
options: Normal, because FVC is above 3 L
questions.why: FEV₁/FVC = 1.5/3.5 ≈ 0.43, below 0.7, so airflow is obstructed (as in asthma or COPD). Calling it restrictive because FVC is reduced ignores the low ratio; a restrictive pattern keeps the ratio normal or high. Calling it normal looks only at FVC and ignores the ratio. A 'high ratio' comes from dividing the wrong way round (FVC/FEV₁ ≈ 2.3); the correct ratio FEV₁/FVC is low, not high.

questions.q: Use the alveolar gas equation to estimate PAO₂ in a healthy person breathing room air at sea level (Patm 101.3 kPa, PH₂O 6.3 kPa, PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa, R 0.8). Then explain what happens to PAO₂ if PaCO₂ rises to 8.0 kPa with no change in inspired oxygen.
markScheme: States PAO₂ = FiO₂(Patm − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/R
Inspired PO₂: 0.21 × 95 = 19.95 kPa
With PaCO₂ 8.0: 19.95 − 10.0 ≈ 9.95 kPa (about 10 kPa)
Explains that hypoventilation raises alveolar CO₂, which displaces O₂, so PAO₂ falls; corrected by giving supplemental oxygen or improving ventilation
questions.modelAnswer: PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (Patm − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/R. The inspired PO₂ after humidification is 0.21 × (101.3 − 6.3) = 0.21 × 95 = 19.95 kPa. Subtracting 5.3/0.8 = 6.63 kPa gives PAO₂ ≈ 13.3 kPa. If PaCO₂ rises to 8.0 kPa, as in hypoventilation, the CO₂ term becomes 8.0/0.8 = 10.0 kPa, so PAO₂ ≈ 19.95 − 10.0 ≈ 10 kPa. Less fresh gas reaches the alveoli, CO₂ accumulates and occupies more of the alveolar gas, and the alveolar (and so arterial) PO₂ falls. Raising FiO₂ can correct the hypoxaemia, but only improved ventilation will lower the CO₂.

questions.q: Heart rate is 75 beats/min, end-diastolic volume 120 mL and end-systolic volume 50 mL. What is the cardiac output?
questions.why: Stroke volume = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = 70 mL, and cardiac output = 75 × 70 = 5,250 mL/min = 5.25 L/min. 9.0 L/min comes from multiplying heart rate by EDV, forgetting that only the stroke volume is ejected. 3.75 L/min comes from multiplying by ESV (the blood left behind). 70 mL/min is the stroke volume alone, not multiplied by rate.

questions.q: A person stands up quickly and blood pressure drops briefly. Which baroreflex response follows?
options: Increased vagal activity and reduced sympathetic activity
Reduced vagal activity and increased sympathetic activity, raising heart rate and causing vasoconstriction
Release of atrial natriuretic peptide to increase salt excretion
Reduced renin release from the kidney
questions.why: Lower pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, so the medulla reduces vagal tone and increases sympathetic output, raising heart rate, contractility and vasoconstriction within seconds. More vagal and less sympathetic activity is the response to a rise in pressure, so that option reverses the reflex. Natriuretic peptide release would lower volume and pressure and is triggered by stretch, not by a fall. Renin release increases, not decreases, when pressure falls, and it acts over minutes to hours rather than within seconds.

questions.q: List the factors that determine stroke volume and explain the Frank–Starling law with a physiological example.
markScheme: Preload (end-diastolic volume/stretch)
Afterload (arterial pressure the ventricle ejects against)
Contractility (inotropy, e.g. sympathetic β₁ stimulation raising Ca²⁺)
Frank–Starling: increased end-diastolic stretch increases force of contraction (more optimal sarcomere overlap/Ca²⁺ sensitivity)
Example: increased venous return (e.g. on lying down or exercise) raises stroke volume, matching right and left output
questions.modelAnswer: Stroke volume depends on preload, afterload and contractility. Preload is the degree of ventricular filling and stretch at the end of diastole. Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject blood, mainly arterial pressure. Contractility is the intrinsic strength of contraction at a given preload, increased, for example, by sympathetic stimulation of β₁ receptors, which raises Ca²⁺ entry. The Frank–Starling law states that, within limits, a greater end-diastolic volume stretches the myocytes and produces a stronger contraction, so stroke volume increases. This lets the heart match output to venous return: when someone lies down or starts exercising, venous return rises, the ventricles fill more, and stroke volume increases automatically. It also keeps the outputs of the right and left ventricles equal over time.

questions.q: Which hormone is released in response to acid entering the duodenum and stimulates bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas?
questions.why: Secretin from duodenal S cells responds to acid and stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice that neutralises it. Gastrin comes from gastric G cells and stimulates acid secretion, the opposite effect. Cholecystokinin responds mainly to fat and protein and stimulates enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction rather than bicarbonate. Somatostatin is inhibitory, reducing gastric and pancreatic secretion.

questions.q: A patient has jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. Where is the problem most likely to be?
options: Reduced hepatic uptake of unconjugated bilirubin
Obstruction of the common bile duct
Increased production of urobilinogen in the gut
questions.why: Pale stools mean bilirubin is not reaching the gut, and dark urine means water-soluble conjugated bilirubin is spilling into the urine: both point to obstruction after conjugation, e.g. a gallstone in the common bile duct. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which is albumin-bound and does not enter urine, and stools are not pale. Reduced hepatic uptake would also raise unconjugated bilirubin, with normal urine colour. Increased gut urobilinogen implies more bilirubin is reaching the gut, which contradicts pale stools.

questions.q: Explain how dietary fat is digested and absorbed.
markScheme: Emulsification by bile salts (and churning) into small droplets
Pancreatic lipase (with colipase) hydrolyses triglycerides to monoglycerides and fatty acids
Products form mixed micelles with bile salts, carried to the brush border
Absorbed into enterocytes; re-esterified to triglycerides and packaged with apoproteins into chylomicrons
Chylomicrons enter lacteals/lymph; bile salts reabsorbed in terminal ileum (enterohepatic circulation)
questions.modelAnswer: Dietary fat is mostly triglyceride, which is insoluble in water. Churning in the stomach and bile salts in the duodenum emulsify it into small droplets, increasing the surface area for enzymes. Pancreatic lipase, helped by colipase, hydrolyses triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids. These products combine with bile salts to form mixed micelles, which carry them to the brush border, where they diffuse into enterocytes. Inside the cell they are re-made into triglycerides and packaged with cholesterol and apoproteins into chylomicrons. Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, so they pass into lacteals and travel in the lymph. Bile salts remain in the lumen and are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum for reuse (enterohepatic circulation).

questions.q: A substance has a urine concentration of 12 mg/mL, a plasma concentration of 0.1 mg/mL and the urine flow rate is 1 mL/min. What is its clearance?
questions.why: Clearance = U × V / P = 12 × 1 / 0.1 = 120 mL/min. 1.2 mL/min comes from multiplying by P instead of dividing (12 × 0.1). 0.0083 mL/min comes from inverting the formula (P / (U × V) = 0.1/12). 12 mL/min simply takes the urine concentration and forgets to divide by the plasma concentration.

questions.q: Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26, PaCO₂ 3.6 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance?
questions.why: pH below 7.35 is acidaemia; the low bicarbonate explains it, so the primary problem is metabolic acidosis, and the low PaCO₂ shows the lungs compensating by blowing off CO₂. Respiratory acidosis would need a raised PaCO₂, not a low one. Metabolic alkalosis would give a high pH and high bicarbonate. Respiratory alkalosis would give a high pH; the low PaCO₂ here is compensation, not the primary cause, because the pH is acidotic.

questions.q: Describe the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and explain how it restores blood pressure after haemorrhage.
markScheme: Stimuli for renin from juxtaglomerular cells: reduced renal perfusion pressure, reduced NaCl at macula densa, sympathetic β₁ activity
Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE (mainly pulmonary) converts it to angiotensin II
Angiotensin II: arteriolar vasoconstriction (↑TPR), efferent constriction maintains GFR, ↑proximal Na⁺ reabsorption
Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone (↑Na⁺ reabsorption via ENaC, water follows), ADH release and thirst
Net effect: raised TPR now and restored blood volume over hours to days
questions.modelAnswer: After a haemorrhage, renal perfusion pressure falls, less NaCl reaches the macula densa and sympathetic activity increases; all three stimulate juxtaglomerular cells to release renin. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen from the liver to angiotensin I, which angiotensin-converting enzyme, largely in pulmonary endothelium, converts to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles, raising total peripheral resistance and blood pressure quickly, and preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole, helping to maintain GFR. It increases Na⁺ reabsorption in the proximal tubule and stimulates the adrenal zona glomerulosa to release aldosterone, which increases Na⁺ reabsorption through ENaC in the collecting duct, with water following. It also promotes ADH release and thirst, so more water is retained and drunk. Together these raise resistance immediately and restore circulating volume over hours to days.

questions.q: A healthy 20-year-old begins a 30-minute run. Describe and explain the cardiovascular and respiratory changes that allow oxygen delivery to working muscle to increase. Include the roles of the autonomic nervous system, local factors and the oxygen dissociation curve.
markScheme: Autonomic: central command and muscle afferents reduce vagal and increase sympathetic outflow; HR and contractility rise (β₁)
Cardiac output rises: HR × SV; SV increased by contractility and Frank–Starling (increased venous return via muscle pump, respiratory pump, venoconstriction)

Redistribution: local metabolic vasodilatation in muscle (↑CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, adenosine, ↓O₂, NO) with sympathetic vasoconstriction in gut/kidney; TPR falls overall; systolic pressure rises, diastolic little changed
Ventilation rises (tidal volume then rate) via central command, muscle/joint receptors and chemoreceptors; arterial PO₂ and PCO₂ stay near normal in moderate exercise
Pulmonary blood flow increases with recruitment/distension of capillaries, improving V/Q and diffusion capacity
Oxygen extraction: right shift of the dissociation curve in muscle (↑PCO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑temperature) increases unloading; widened arteriovenous O₂ difference (Fick)
Accurate physiology, integration of systems and use of equations (CO = HR × SV; Fick)
Clear structure and correct terminology
questions.modelAnswer:
Oxygen delivery to muscle depends on cardiac output, the share of output reaching muscle, arterial oxygen content and how much oxygen the muscle extracts. Running increases each of these except arterial content, which is held nearly constant.

Autonomic changes. At the start of exercise, central command from the motor cortex and feedback from muscle and joint receptors act on the medullary cardiovascular centres. Vagal activity falls and sympathetic activity rises. Heart rate increases (β₁ effects on the SA node) and contractility increases (β₁ effects raising Ca²⁺ entry into myocytes). The baroreflex is reset to operate around a higher pressure.

Cardiac output. Since CO = HR × SV, both factors rise. Stroke volume increases because of greater contractility and greater preload: the skeletal muscle pump squeezes veins, deeper breathing lowers intrathoracic pressure (the respiratory pump), and sympathetic venoconstriction moves blood centrally. By the Frank–Starling law, greater end-diastolic stretch gives a stronger contraction. Cardiac output can rise several-fold.

Redistribution of flow. In active muscle, local metabolites (raised CO₂, H⁺, K⁺ and adenosine, low O₂, plus nitric oxide) dilate arterioles and open more capillaries, overriding sympathetic constriction there. Elsewhere, especially gut and kidney, sympathetic vasoconstriction reduces flow, and skin flow later rises for heat loss. Because muscle vasodilatation is so large, total peripheral resistance falls; systolic pressure rises with the increased output while diastolic pressure changes little.

Respiratory changes. Ventilation rises at once through central command and limb receptor input, then is fine-tuned by chemoreceptors and rising CO₂ production. Tidal volume increases first, then rate, so alveolar ventilation rises in proportion to CO₂ output and arterial PO₂ and PCO₂ stay close to normal during moderate exercise. Increased pulmonary blood flow recruits and distends capillaries, improving V/Q matching and the effective area for diffusion, so blood is still fully oxygenated despite a shorter transit time.

Oxygen unloading. In working muscle, raised PCO₂, H⁺ (the Bohr effect) and temperature shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen at a given PO₂. Muscle PO₂ also falls, moving down the steep part of the curve. The arteriovenous oxygen difference therefore widens. By the Fick principle (O₂ consumption = CO × arteriovenous O₂ difference), the rise in oxygen use is met by both a higher cardiac output and greater extraction.

Together, these coordinated autonomic, local and respiratory responses raise oxygen delivery and use many-fold while keeping arterial blood gases stable.

questions.q: A man is lost in a hot desert without water for 24 hours. Explain how his body acts to limit the fall in body water and maintain blood pressure. Include hypothalamic, pituitary, adrenal and renal mechanisms.
markScheme: Water loss (sweat, insensible, urine) raises plasma osmolality and reduces blood volume
Hypothalamic osmoreceptors stimulate thirst and ADH release from posterior pituitary (made in supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei)
ADH acts on V₂ receptors: aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting duct; with medullary gradient (countercurrent multiplier) produces small volume of concentrated urine
Reduced volume/pressure: baroreceptor unloading increases sympathetic activity (vasoconstriction, HR) and further ADH release
Renin release (reduced perfusion, macula densa, β₁) → angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, efferent constriction, proximal Na⁺ reabsorption, thirst, ADH)
Aldosterone from zona glomerulosa increases Na⁺ (and water) reabsorption via ENaC; natriuretic peptides fall
Limits: obligatory water loss continues; correct identification of feedback loops
questions.modelAnswer:
Over 24 hours in heat he loses water through sweating, breathing and urine. Because sweat is hypotonic, plasma osmolality rises; at the same time plasma volume and, eventually, blood pressure fall. The body responds to both signals.

Osmotic response. Osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus detect the rise in osmolality. They stimulate thirst and cause neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, which make ADH, to release it from their terminals in the posterior pituitary. ADH binds V₂ receptors on collecting duct principal cells, triggering insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane. Water then moves out of the duct into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, created by the countercurrent multiplier of the loop of Henle and urea recycling. The result is a small volume of concentrated urine, conserving water. ADH at higher levels also constricts arterioles.

Volume and pressure responses. Falling blood volume reduces stretch of atrial receptors and arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. The medulla increases sympathetic activity, raising heart rate and causing vasoconstriction in skin, gut and kidney, which supports blood pressure. Reduced stretch also adds a non-osmotic stimulus to ADH release and reduces natriuretic peptide secretion, so less sodium is excreted.

Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. Reduced renal perfusion pressure, lower NaCl delivery to the macula densa and sympathetic β₁ stimulation all increase renin release from juxtaglomerular cells. Renin forms angiotensin I from angiotensinogen, and ACE converts this to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles (raising peripheral resistance), constricts the efferent arteriole (helping to keep GFR adequate), increases sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule, and stimulates thirst and ADH release. It also stimulates the adrenal zona glomerulosa to secrete aldosterone, which increases sodium reabsorption through ENaC in the collecting duct; water follows sodium where ADH has made the duct permeable.

Limits. Sweating for cooling and insensible losses continue, and the kidney must still excrete a minimum urine volume to clear solutes, so these mechanisms only slow the loss. Without water intake, volume continues to fall, and the balance between conserving water and losing heat by sweating becomes critical.
